title: Why Does a Tomato Turn Red? Explained Simply | PUC Biology Class 11
description:
A green tomato sat on the kitchen shelf on Monday, and by Thursday it had turned bright red. Diya asks: where did the green go, and where did the red come from? The answer is a tiny part inside plant cells called a plastid, and its partner in almost every cell, the mitochondrion.

You will see what an organelle and a double membrane are, then a zoom ladder from a cell to one mitochondrion, its cristae and its matrix (circular DNA, RNA, 70S ribosomes). Watch aerobic respiration pack energy into ATP, then the chloroplast labelled (stroma, thylakoids, grana, stroma lamellae), chromoplasts in a ripening tomato and the three leucoplasts. Then mitochondria vs chloroplasts side by side, a pause and think about the potato, six parts sorted, the 70S ribosome exam trap, an original NEET-pattern question with a full solution, a recap card and three questions.

This is Episode 65 of our PUC Biology series.

Made for NCERT, CBSE, ISC (CISCE), PUC (Karnataka) and NEET students.

In this video:
0:00 A tomato turns red
0:34 Organelles and the double membrane
0:58 Zoom ladder: cell, mitochondrion, cristae, matrix
1:41 How a mitochondrion makes ATP
2:17 Chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts
3:12 Mitochondria vs chloroplasts + pause and think
3:56 Worked example: six parts
4:22 Exam trap: 80S or 70S?
4:45 Practice question (NEET pattern)
5:08 Recap and three questions to answer

Next episode: Ribosomes, Cytoskeleton, Cilia, Flagella and Centrosome. How can tiny hairs on a cell sweep dust out of your windpipe?
